newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-New data give scant hope for Russian economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New data give scant hope for Russian economy.

text.p: The Russian government confirmed a downward revision of its economic forecasts on Tuesday, pointing to lower output, lower gross domestic product (GDP) and lower investment this year.

Government figures distributed at the State Duma lower house of parliament on Tuesday showed that industrial output and GDP could fall by up to two percent in 1997, while agricultural output and investment could be five percent below 1996 levels.

"Taking into account forecast growth rates for agricultural output, investment, exports and imports, GDP...is forecast at 2,550-2,600 trillion roubles ($449.4 billion), or 130-180 trillion lower than seen in the law on the federal budget," a government paper said.

The forecasts, and the official confirmation that Russia's long-awaited economic turnaround is still far away, are the latest problem for the government as it tries to persuade Duma deputies to approve painful plans to cut spending.
Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov told reporters that parliament would debate the plans on June 11.
The debate was originally due last month, but deputies postponed it until after the Duma's latest recess, asking the government to provide more information about its plans.

Ministers, who say spending cuts are essential to cope with dismal tax revenues, had originally forecast growth in GDP and industrial output of up to two percent and a two percent decline in agricultural production.
But they started admitting in recent weeks that the economy might not grow at all.

In the latest document, issued by First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais in response to the Duma request, the government said output in the large and medium-sized enterprises which formed the backbone of the Soviet-era economy would fall three percent.
But the document said overall output would be flat or two percent below 1996 levels, taking into account likely growth in smaller firms and in the hard-to-measure shadow economy.
Chubais, Russia's one-time privatisation chief who is now masterminding reforms, has vowed to press on with painful policies designed to squeeze inflation out of the economy.
"We cannot wait, the economy and the people cannot wait. That's why we have such a tough position," he told Kommersant Daily newspaper in an interview published on Tuesday.
He warned of calamity if the lower house rejected the tax code, upon which the government wants to base its 1998 budget to put the state finances on to a sounder footing.

Chubais said the government was "ready to reach a compromise" with the Duma, where communists and their allies can block legislation, although they have little power to unseat the government without risking dissolution by Yeltsin.
Chubais is also trying to force recaltricant tax debtors to pay their bills, highlighting a spiral of non-payments as one of Russia's toughest economic problems.

Russian economic output has declined stubbornly in the 5-1/2 years since Moscow launched its first economic reform programme and forecasts of growth have proved wrong time and again. $1=RUR 5,785 ($ = 5786 Russian Roubles)
